speech.text: Corn Rock Light stands on a stack of black stone, nine miles out to sea. No road, no bridge, one iron ladder bolted to the cliff. You took the quietest job on the coast, thirty days alone. Service the lens, check the batteries, sign the log. The supply boat drops you at dawn. Captain Brandt swings your crates onto the landing and taps his watch. Thirty days, I'll be back on the thirtieth. Keep the kettle warm. His engine fades. Then there is only the swell, slapping the rock. You climb the ladder. Eighteen feet, straight up, above the highest tide. Then a steel door. Then a spiral stair of iron. A hundred and forty steps to the lamp room. You check what you have. Twenty tins of food, rice, tea, salt. A tank under the floor. Three hundred liters of rainwater. A marine radio, four flares, a rope, a toolbox. For thirty days, it's plenty. That night lens begins to turn. One flash every 15 seconds. So every captain knows which light he is looking at. You fall asleep to the hum of its motor. It is the last normal night of your life. Day one. The silence. At six radio wakes you. Channel 16. The one every ship is supposed to listen to. Voices overlapping. A coast guard operator. Talking too fast. All vessels, stay off the coast. Do not land. Repeat, do not. Static. You call back. Nothing. By noon, even the static is gone. That night, you climb to the gallery, the narrow iron balcony around the lamp. On the horizon, the coast is a smear of orange. Cities glow in the dark. You can see it from across the sea. You watch it for an hour. Then a patch goes dark. Then another. other. One district at a time. Like someone walking through a house, switching off the lamps. By midnight, the horizon is black. Nobody is coming to tell you why. Day three. The trawler. At dawn, a fishing boat drifts out of the haze. Engine dead. Nets trailing. Sliding sideways on the current. You raise the binoculars. Figures on the deck. Shoulder to shoulder. Swaying with the roll. Gray faces. Mouths slightly open. Nobody at the wheel. Nobody steering. The boat is just going wherever the sea sends it. The sea sends it here. At ten past seven, the hull grinds onto the rocky shelf under the cliff. The whole tower shivers. They step off the deck, one after another. Thirty -one of them. You count twice. They gather at the foot of the ladder. Hands Hands reach for the rungs. Slide off. Reach again. They can't climb. It's the first good news you've had in three days. Then your elbow knocks the mug off the sill. It rings off the iron stair. Below the window, thirty -one heads snap around. Not up at you. Down. At the rock. They aren't looking for you. They're listening through their feet. You tap the iron rail with one fingernail. Every one of them turns toward the tower wall. wall. Sound travels through iron about 15 times faster than through air. And this tower is 140 steps of iron, bolted into solid stone. It isn't a lighthouse. It's a drum. You tear a blanket into strips and wrap your boots. Wool soaks up vibration. You learn to walk heel first. Weight in your hips. You chalk a rule on the lamproom wall. Rule one. Walk soft. You set every tin down like it's made of glass. For the first time in your life, you're afraid of your own feet. Day five. The water. On the fifth morning, you taste the tank. Salt. During the night, a wave through spray over the overflow pipe and into the rain gutter. Don't drink it. Seawater is about three and a half percent salt. Your body needs extra water to flush that out. Every cup takes more than it gives. Drink the sea, and you die of thirst. Faster. You search the crates. Bottled water. Forty liters. At three liters a day, 13 days. You need rain. One millimeter of rain on one square meter of roof is one liter of water. The lamproom roof is about 40 square meters. 10 millimeters of rain is 400 liters. You split a drain pipe into a gutter and run it to an empty barrel. You build a still from a bowl, a sheet of plastic, and a stone. Sun heats the seawater. Vapor rises. Drops run down into a cup. A cup a day. Rule two, never drink the sea. Day eight, the barometer. On day eight, the barometer in the storeroom starts to fall. A drop of more than six millibars in three hours means a gale is coming. This one drops nine. By evening, the waves are climbing the cliff and falling back in sheets of white. Force nine. Spray hits the lamproom glass hundred feet above the sea. Under the cliff, the crowd at the foot of the ladder doesn't shelter. They just stand there, taking it. Then the rain arrives. It hammers the roof. It races down the gutter. You hear the barrel filling. By morning, it's full. You stand on the gallery with your face up and drink straight from the sky. Water, 250 liters. Food, 12 tins. The storm has also moved the trawler. Only a few feet. You don't notice. Day 10. The rock pools. Food. 20 tins sounds like a lot, but one tin a day isn't enough to keep your hands steady, and you've been eating too. Day 10. Ten tins left. The sea will have to feed you. The east side of the rock is a shelf of black stone and shallow pools. The crowd is at the ladder on the west. Between you, a hundred feet of cliff. You wait for low tide. At low tide, the pools open up like a pantry. The waves are loud enough to swallow your footsteps, so you go down at dawn in wool -wrapped boots. Limpets cling to the rock like small stone hats. A knife flicks them off. Cooked, they're safe. Mussels, you leave. In warm months, they can carry toxins that cooking doesn't destroy. Dulse, a red seaweed, floats in the pools. Dried, it's chewy and salty and safe. You drop a hand line off the ledge with a bent nail and a scrap of limpet. 20 minutes later, a pollock as long as your forearm flaps on the stone. It isn't feast. But it's the first thing in 10 days that didn't come out of a tin. Day 13. The voice. A handheld radio can only see as far as the horizon. Radio waves travel in straight lines. The higher the antenna, the farther the horizon. From the top of a 40 -meter tower, you can reach about 17 miles. So every night at 8, you call. Koran Rock. Koran Rock. Anyone. 12 nights. Static. 12 nights of of your own voice going out into nothing. On the 13th, a voice. Calm. A woman. Close. Coran Rock, this is Harrowhead. My name is Mara. Say again. You're alive? You grip the radio so hard your knuckles ache. She was Coast Guard. She's in the old station with five others. They have a boat. Fuel for one run. We'll come for you on the 30th, if the sea lets us. Then she says one more thing. Keep your lamp burning, Coran. We can see it from here. You look up at the lens. ends. Nobody ever told you anyone was watching. Day 16. The knocking. Every keeper signs the log. You flip back through 20 years of entries. In six different hands. Six different winters. The same line. Knocking on the stairs at dusk. Checked. Nothing there. Tonight, at dusk, you hear it. You freeze on the stair with one wool boot in the air. It's coming from the rail. You follow it up, step by step. Then you lay your palm on the cold iron. Metal shrinks as it cools. After a hot day, a stair like this creaks and ticks all evening like a house settling. It's only the iron. You laugh, quietly. Then at three in the morning, you wake to a different knocking. Slow, heavy, wood against stone. The iron has been cold for hours. Day 19, the lamp. The lamp room is dimmer than it was. The battery gauge reads 40%. The tower runs on solar panels and a small wind turbine. You climb out onto the roof and find the panels crusted white. Salt spray dries on the glass and blocks the sun. The turbine is worse. The blades have stopped. The bearing has seized. Rain washes the panels clean. Sea water only makes it worse. So you carry up two buckets from the barrel, and you scrub with a rag. You grease the turbine bearing from the toolbox. You free the blades with a broom handle. They turn. By evening, the gauge climbs. The lens beam reaches 20 miles. Mara said they can see it. Rule three. The light stays lit. Whatever else you do, you never let it fail. Somewhere across the water, six people are steering by it. They have never met you. They are already counting on you. Day 22. The ramp. At dawn, you hear it. Slow. Heavy. Wood against stone. The knocking from day 16 was never the iron. You look down over the gallery rail. The trawler has shifted. The swell has pushed it. A little more every night. Now its bow lifts and falls against the cliff, right beneath the ladder platform. The deck is a ramp. The crowd climbs it, not like climbing a ladder, just walking up a slope, one after another. They reach the platform, they reach the steel door, then they start to pound. The whole tower hums like a struck bell, the iron rings under your feet, the rail shivers in your hand. You can't sleep, you can't cook, you can't talk. Three nights you sit in the lamp room with wool in your ears. The door holds, they can't turn a handle, but nobody told you that the worst sound in the world is a crowd that never gets tired. Day 25, the plan. On day 25, you open the tide table. Full moon in three days. That full moon and new moon, the sun and the moon pull together. Tides rise higher and fall lower. They're called spring tides, and they come every fortnight. On day 28, the sea will climb higher than it has all month. You have 40 meters of anchor chain in the storeroom. They follow noise, so you will give them noise. You will hang the chain from the west gallery and let it bang against the cliff. They'll leave the door. They'll walk down the ramp. They'll shuffle out along the low west ledge, the lowest stone on the whole rock, to the sound. And on that ledge, at the top of a spring tide, a set of waves will do the rest. They can't swim. Once the water closes over them, they sink. If you get it wrong, they stay at the door. If you get it right, you'll have to make more noise than you have made in 25 days. days. Day 28. The chain. High water is at 20 to 7. You carry the chain up in your arms, link by link, wrapped in cloth. At half past 6, you lower it over the west rail. You let go. back down the bow, onto the ledge, and along the stone toward the sound. 31 of them, packed together, shoulder to shoulder, arms hanging. You wait. The first wave slaps their knees. The second climbs to their waists. The third comes out of the dark like a wall. When it falls back, the ledge is empty. Then the bow of the trawler groans and slides off the cliff into the black. The sea closes. The rock is quiet. For the first time in 25 days, nobody is knocking. You sit down on the cold iron and you cry. Day 29. The oars. Fog. It rolls in before dawn and swallows the sea. The beam turns through it. A white arm in a gray room. At five, the radio. Corrin, this is Harrow. We're in the water. Mara's voice is a whisper. We're rowing the last mile. No engine. We know about the sound. You stand on the gallery. You don't breathe. You can't see anything. Only fog and the white beam going round, lighting nothing. Somewhere below, a boat is looking for the rock and all you can do is keep the light turning. Then you hear it. A small, wet sound. Far off. cliff. Six people. Worn faces. Blistered hands. Mara looks up at you. Fifty. Gray hair. Salt on her coat. You kept your lamp burning, she says. She holds up a flask of tea. Thirty days, you say. She nods. She doesn't say, you look terrible. She doesn't have to. Brant's boat was tied up in the cove at Harrow. Empty. He never made it back. You think of a man swinging your crates onto the landing, tapping his watch. Keep the kettle warm. You look down at the ladder. She says the rest quietly. There were 11 lights on this coast. One by one, they went dark. Yours is the only one that never did. You look back at Corrin Rock. At the lens. At the chalk on the lamp room wall. Mall. Walk soft. Never drink the sea. The light stays lit. Ten more towers, Mara says. Ten dark lamps. Somebody has to climb them.
